candidates.note: Cross-bearing funerary stela inscribed in Greek, “There is one God who helps. Dios.” Dios is a personal name, possibly abbreviated from Dioscoros. The object is a stela only; no human remains are represented.
candidates.source_description: Round-topped rectangular limestone stela. The architectural decoration consists of a hemisphere bounded by a guilloche spiral within the circuit of the stela, the whole being supported by two end-pillars flanking a central Maltese cross. The upper left side, which is shown in an early photo (Rustafjaell 1909, pl. 35) is now missing. Below the whole, is cut one line of Greek text reading εἷς θεός ὁ βοηθῶν Διὁς (there is one God who helps. Dios). The latter is a personal name, which may be an abbreviated form of Dios(coros), the name of two of the Coptic church's patriarchs. Previously part of the collection of Robert de Rustafjaell, which was sold at auction (lot 88) in 1907. It was purchased by the dealer Lawrence before becoming part of the Kent collection. Bequeathed to Harrogate Museum in 1968. According to Rustafjaell, the stela comes from the neighbourhood of Thebes. It dates to the Fourth–Seventh century AD.

candidates.source_description:
This is a Zapotec funerary effigy, a characteristic ceramic form produced in the Valley of Oaxaca during the Classic period, closely associated with the city of Monte Albán, one of the earliest major urban centers in the Americas. These figures were placed in tombs alongside other solid vessels and urns as part of funerary and ancestor-veneration practices. This piece in particular depicts the features of Cocijo, the most important deity in the Zapotec pantheon, associated with rain, lightning, thunder, and by extension agricultural fertility. Due to the priestly garb, it’s likely this is an individual bearing Cocijo’s mask/attributes rather than a literal portrait of the god. Provenience unknown.

candidates.note: Comparable light wooden stools or pedestals (odo Shango) serve in shrines to Shango and in priestly initiation. The source carefully says objects similar to this one may have served these roles, so retain that qualification.
candidates.source_description:
The scan of *Yoruba Stool* (1981.012.345) from the [Grinnell College Museum of Art](https://www.grinnell.edu/campus-life/arts-culture/museum) was made on 10/01/2024 with the Creaform Academia 50 handheld 3D scanner and edited in VXelements and VXModel 10 with minor texture map editing and converting done in GIMP. Unknown [Yoruba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yoruba_people) artist, n.d. Wood and pigment. Gift of Jack Baruch.

Objects similar to this light-weight, ovoid wooden Yoruba stool or pedestal (*odo Shnago*) may serve important functions both in shrines to honor [Shango](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shango), the deity associated with thunder and lightning, in initiation rituals for the Shango priesthood. A stool of this type was customarily used as a seat on which novitiates sat to have their heads shaved during their last day of initiation. Other ritual items associated with Shango worship, such as neolithic double-axe shaped stones, are placed on top of these stools when not in use.

candidates.title: Gable Figure from the Hieron of the Samothracian Mysteries
candidates.geography: Sanctuary of the Great Gods, Samothrace, Greece
candidates.subject: Samothracian mystery-cult context
candidates.original_location: North gable of the Hieron, Samothrace, Greece
candidates.source_institution: iedu360.eu; object in the Ephesos Museum, Vienna
candidates.attribution: 3D model “A Marble Figure from the Samothracian Mysteries” by iedu360.eu (iedu360.eu), via Sketchfab, CC BY 4.0. Atrium serves an optimized derivative.
candidates.scan_source: Institutional or documented museum-object 3D model via Sketchfab
candidates.note: Cult-building context is secure, but the figure’s identity is interpretive: one proposal sees her as a personification of Samothrace’s principal mountain, not as a deity. She originally held a drinking vessel.
candidates.source_description:
Encased Woman: 
This marble figure, originating from the Hellenistic period (150-125 BC), was part of the decoration of the north gable of the "Hieron" on the island of Samothrace. While the Hieron was likely not a temple, it served as a place where mystics were initiated into the mystery cults. The reclining female figure rests her right hand on a rock, her cloak slipping down to her hips. She originally held a drinking vessel in her left hand, which was lost over time.

One interpretation suggests that the gable depicted the founding of the Samothracian mysteries by Aetion, with the female figure symbolizing the island's main mountain. This exquisite piece offers a glimpse into the artistic traditions and spiritual practices of ancient Greece.

Now part of the Ephesos Museum in Vienna, this figure was acquired during the Austrian Expedition led by Prof. Conze in 1874.
